analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, housing, credit, and public accommodations.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 224-206 in February 2021, but the Senate never held a vote and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Equality Act would write sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination into the nation's core civil rights laws, covering jobs, housing, credit, schools, jury service, and businesses open to the public. It would also state that discrimination based on pregnancy or sex stereotypes is sex discrimination, and would remove a religious-freedom law as a defense to violating these rules. The House passed it almost entirely along party lines in February 2021, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ people and women would gain clear, enforceable federal protections against being fired, refused housing, denied credit, or turned away from stores, shelters, health care providers, and other public-facing businesses because of who they are.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations, education, federal funding, and the jury system.

The bill text cites evidence that same-sex couples seeking housing get fewer positive responses from landlords, that transgender people have about half the homeownership rate of non-transgender people, and that about 1 in 5 transgender people experience homelessness.

The bill states that federal law already prohibits sex discrimination, citing the Supreme Court's 2020 Bostock decision holding that firing workers for being gay or transgender is sex discrimination, and makes that protection explicit across civil rights statutes rather than leaving it to courts.

It bars denial of access to restrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms consistent with a person's gender identity, and expands the definition of public accommodations to include online retailers, stores, salons, shelters, health care providers, and transportation services.
It codifies that pregnancy, childbirth, and related medical conditions cannot receive less favorable treatment than other physical conditions.

analysis.who_pays: Religiously affiliated schools, adoption and foster care agencies, and other service providers would lose the ability to claim a religious-freedom defense under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act when accused of discrimination. Businesses including online retailers and small service providers would face the same nondiscrimination rules as hotels and restaurants, with legal liability for refusing service.
analysis.who_pays_short: Religiously affiliated institutions and covered businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill states that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act 'shall not provide a claim concerning, or a defense to a claim under' any covered civil rights title, so religiously affiliated schools, charities, and individuals could not invoke religious liberty to decline to follow the new rules.

It expands public accommodations to 'any establishment that provides a good, service, or program,' including online retailers and service providers, with no small-business exemption, exposing a much wider range of enterprises to discrimination suits.
It requires access to shared facilities such as restrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity, a rule opponents contested throughout the debate.

The bill carries no carve-outs for faith-based child welfare providers even though the bill text acknowledges many child-placing agencies refuse to serve same-sex couples; those agencies would have to choose between compliance and exiting the field.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For LGBTQ people and women the protections are concrete: a landlord, lender, or store that turns them away today often faces no federal penalty, and this bill would change that. The cost falls on a different axis: religiously affiliated institutions would lose statutory religious-liberty defenses, and a much broader set of businesses would face liability. The bill's design choice with no exceptions or phase-ins for religious providers is the reason opposition was intense enough to stop it; supporters judged that trade acceptable, opponents did not, and the Senate never resolved it.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 224-206 in February 2021, was placed on the Senate calendar two days later, received a single Judiciary Committee hearing, and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on February 25, 2021, by a vote of 224 to 206, with all 221 voting Democrats in favor and only 3 of 211 voting Republicans joining them.
The Senate received the bill on March 1, 2021, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 9.
The Senate Judiciary Committee held a hearing on the bill on March 17, 2021.
No further action was recorded in the Senate for the rest of the 117th Congress; the bill never received a floor vote, a committee vote, or a motion to proceed.

With 50 Senate Republicans and a chamber where 60 votes are normally needed to end debate on most legislation, the bill's supporters never assembled the votes to bring it to a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the bill came out ahead: religiously affiliated institutions, faith-based child welfare providers, and other objectors kept the existing legal landscape, where no federal statute explicitly bans sexual orientation or gender identity discrimination in housing, credit, or public accommodations. LGBTQ people remained reliant on a patchwork of state laws and court decisions such as Bostock for employment only.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bill opponents; no federal statute changed

for.name: David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Equality Act and guided it to House passage; moved to table the motion to reconsider after the vote.

for.name: 221 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously (221-0 among Democrats voting) to pass the bill on final passage.

for.name: 3 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Joined all Democrats to vote for final passage.

against.name: 206 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 206 of 211 voting Republicans against.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote in the two years it sat on the calendar, despite Democrats holding a majority.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Equality Act as written and opposed carving exceptions to the Senate filibuster, which would have been required to pass it over Republican objections.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no support for the bill; without them, supporters would have needed to change Senate debate rules to reach a vote, which did not happen.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, all 221 voting Democrats supported the bill and 206 of 211 voting Republicans opposed it; only 3 Republicans crossed over, and the bill never reached a Senate vote.

industries.industry: Religiously affiliated service providers (schools, adoption and foster agencies, hospitals)
industries.note: The bill removes the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense under the covered civil rights titles, so these providers could no longer refuse service to LGBTQ people on religious grounds. Their interest in keeping that exemption runs directly against the people the bill protects.

industries.industry: Retail, online commerce, and consumer service businesses
industries.note: The bill expands 'public accommodations' to cover any provider of goods, services, or programs, including online retailers, salons, banks, and shelters, creating new liability for businesses that turn customers away. Many businesses already serve all customers voluntarily, but objectors would lose that option.
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act would add sexual orientation and gender identity to its prohibited bases, so lenders could no longer deny mortgages, credit cards, or student loans on those grounds.

The bill largely codifies the Supreme Court's 2020 Bostock ruling, which already treats anti-LGBTQ firing as sex discrimination, so the practical change for most employers is modest; the bill mainly locks the rule into statute where courts could not revisit it.
